cards.front: Recall a key point about Vocabulary & English Derivatives
cards.back: The Defined Vocabulary List (DVL) contains the words that may appear in GCSE Latin translation exams — approximately 400-500 words depending on the board.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Vocabulary & English Derivatives
cards.back: Learning Latin vocabulary through English derivatives is highly effective: e.g. ambulare (to walk) → ambulance; videre (to see) → video; scribere (to write) → scribe/script.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Vocabulary & English Derivatives
cards.back: Common Latin prefixes: trans- (across → transport), sub- (under → submarine), pre- (before → predict), re- (back/again → return), ex/e- (out of → export).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Vocabulary & English Derivatives
cards.back: Common Latin suffixes: -tion (action/state from verb stems → narration from narro), -al (pertaining to → naval from navis), -ous (full of → furious from furia).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Vocabulary & English Derivatives
cards.back: Many English words come directly from Latin: aqua (water → aquatic), luna (moon → lunar), stella (star → stellar), terra (earth → terrestrial).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Vocabulary & English Derivatives
cards.back: Legal and scientific vocabulary is heavily Latin-based: habeas corpus, subpoena, pro bono, quorum; and binomial nomenclature (Homo sapiens, Canis lupus).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Vocabulary & English Derivatives
cards.back: The OCR DVL is published in the specification and must be memorised — words outside the DVL are glossed in the exam.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Vocabulary & English Derivatives
cards.back: Learning noun-adjective pairs together helps retention: puella bona (good girl), vir fortis (brave man), bellum magnum (great war).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Vocabulary & English Derivatives
cards.back: Important high-frequency words: sum (to be), habeo (to have), dico (to say), facio (to make/do), venio (to come), video (to see), mitto (to send).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Vocabulary & English Derivatives
cards.back: Latin abbreviations survive in English: etc. (et cetera), i.e. (id est), e.g. (exempli gratia), N.B. (nota bene), vs. (versus), a.m. (ante meridiem), p.m. (post meridiem).

cards.front: What should you know about gcse latin exam tips — vocabulary & english derivatives?
cards.back: 1. For Vocabulary & English Derivatives, use a range of vocabulary and complex grammatical structures to access higher marks 2. Check verb tenses, agreements and word order carefully in your written work 3. In translation tasks, translate meaning rather than word-for-word 4. When writing about Vocabulary & English Derivatives, include opinions and justifications, not just descriptions 5. For listening and reading, focus on key words and cognates to extract meaning
Explain how Latin vocabulary has influenced English, giving at least six specific examples of derivatives from different Latin roots. (6 marks)
